description:
Hi, I’m AR, an AI/ML engineer from Colombo, competing solo in the Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map challenge.

My plan is to build an interactive Mars map that helps future astronauts plan safe, science-rich Marswalks. It will combine NASA Mars mission data (CTX and HiRISE imagery, MOLA elevation) with a computer vision model that detects hazards like boulders, craters and steep slopes. A route planner then finds the safest path between points while passing interesting science stops.
summary: A-ROUTE is a Mars exploration platform built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. It brings together real Mars terrain data, rover observations, panorama images, drill locations, and weather records to make exploring Mars more interactive. Users can explore the 3D surfaces of Gale and Jezero craters, examine elevation, slope, and contour layers, and plan routes based on fastest or safest terrain conditions using adjustable parameters. The platform also includes a first-person exploration mode where users can visit rover locations and investigate scientific findings through missions. By bringing maps, scientific data, and exploration together, A-ROUTE offers a more hands-on way to understand Mars and the discoveries made by its robotic explorers.
details:
A-ROUTE

A cinematic entry, a destination selector, a shared scientific 3-D workspace for Gale and Jezero crater, terrain-aware route planning over published elevation models, and a first-person surface mode on the same data.

Abdul Raheem Aouffan (Team Leader & Member)

GitHub Repository: https://github.com/abdulraheem05/A-Route

1. Overview

A-ROUTE is a web application that turns published Mars orbital data into a place you can explore, measure and plan in. It opens with a cinematic view of the planet, lets you pick a landing site from eight catalogued destinations, and drops you into a workspace with two modes: MAP, an orbital 3-D explorer with real elevation, real imagery, layers, an inspector and terrain-aware route planning; and PLAY, first-person exploration of the same ground with missions built from published mission results.

Two craters are open — Gale and Jezero — and they share one renderer, one camera system, one panel set and one terrain pipeline, driven by a crater configuration object. The rule the whole project follows is that every value on screen names the dataset it came from and whether it is measured, derived, interpreted or simulated, and anything the data cannot support is said plainly rather than filled in.

2. Features

2.1 The Scientific 3D Map

  • Real Terrain: Elevation from published DEMs — Gale 2405 × 2232 cells, Jezero 2204 × 2098, both at 100 m — rendered as a 1.16 M-vertex mesh with vertical exaggeration always shown.
  • Live Orbital Imagery: NASA Mars Trek CTX draped over the terrain, with HiRISE detail patches loading as a window around the camera as you zoom in, to about 0.3 m per pixel.
  • Layer Tree: Four collapsible groups — Surface, Terrain Analysis, Exploration, Geology — with per-layer visibility, legend and opacity. Hillshade, elevation tint, slope and contours at a settable interval are computed from the loaded DEM.
  • Click-Anywhere Inspector: Latitude, longitude, elevation, slope with the grid spacing it was measured over, the dataset actually sampled, the nearest waypoint and distance to the traverse.
  • Rover Layers: The published traverse where one exists, drive-end waypoints, IAU landmarks and mission or drill sites, all positioned from the rover's own record.
  • Sol Timeline: Scrub the mission by sol; the rover marker, the readouts and the weather panel follow.
  • Weather Panel: Observed daily summaries from Curiosity's REMS or Perseverance's MEDA, for the sols the feed actually returned.
  • Camera: Orbit, pan, zoom, touch pinch, fit-the-crater, coordinate search and a home view, clamped to the crater's bounds.

2.2 Measure & Plan — Terrain-Aware Routing

One pair of points does two jobs: the straight line between them is the measurement, and the same pair is the input to route planning.

  • Pick Points: Click the terrain — the picker intersects the elevation data, not the drawn mesh — or use a searchable index of places the crater already loads: landing sites, the rover's position at the selected sol, IAU features and mission sites.
  • Two Routes, One Search: A* with eight-connected moves runs over a window of the elevation grid already in memory, decimated to stay under 90,000 nodes, with the effective cell size reported. Fastest minimises travel time and will climb where climbing is quicker; safest multiplies the same cost by a penalty rising with slope and refuses anything above the safe limit, buying gentler ground with extra distance.
  • Honest Numbers: Elevation, slope, distance, gain and loss are measured from the DEM. The drive pace is derived from the rover's own record — 17.4 m/sol over sols 13–2006 for Perseverance, odometry-based for Curiosity — not invented. The slope limits and the slope-speed curve are adjustable assumptions, and the panel says so.
  • No-Data Is Impassable: Nothing is interpolated across a gap, and if an endpoint has no coverage the planner refuses instead of guessing a path.
  • Drawn on the Ground: Routes follow the rendered surface, fastest in orange and safest in green, with the direct line dashed grey so it is never mistaken for a plan. Hovering the elevation profile rings the matching place on the terrain.

2.3 PLAY — Surface Exploration

First person on the same elevation data, as a suited human rather than a rover: eye height 1.7 m, walk 1.4 m/s, run 3.4 m/s, Mars gravity 3.72 m/s², a walkable slope limit and an interaction radius at each site.

  • Missions: Gale has 10 missions spanning sols 3–3565; Jezero has 10 missions with 18 objectives.
  • Sourced Science Entries: 10 for Gale and 19 for Jezero.
  • Panorama Mosaics: 8 for Gale and 45 for Jezero.
  • Targets with a Published Image: 3 of 10 for Gale and 0 of 19 for Jezero.

Every site is placed by resolving the rover's own traverse at that sol; if the traverse cannot be loaded the game says so instead of guessing. Inspection shows the real image with an Inspect button, runs a visible sweep, and only then records the objective — opening a popup completes nothing — and a target with no published image says exactly that. Panorama coverage is claimed only where NASA publishes it, and progress saves per crater.

2.4 Provenance, Built into the Interface

  • A Dataset Registry You Can Open: Fifteen datasets, each with instrument, mission, resolution, coverage, units, limitations, citation and use. Clicking any dataset tag in the app opens its entry.
  • Four Evidence Classes: Measured (CTX and HiRISE imagery, REMS and MEDA summaries), derived (DEMs, slope, hillshade, profiles, rover localisation), interpreted (geologic units, feature names) and simulated (routing assumptions, the rendered PLAY surface). No value is shown without its class.
  • Stated Absence: The layer panel has a “Not available” group: Jezero's geologic polygons, a verified Mars 2020 traverse path, weather for most sols and 1 m rover-region elevation each appear as a row with its reason.
  • Terrain Stops Where the Data Stop: No-data cells are discarded in the shader rather than coloured, so you see a dark gap, not invented ground — which matters for Jezero, where stereo coverage reaches 20.6% of the display region.

3. Data and How It Reaches the Screen

The expensive work happens once, offline: a documented Python script clips, reprojects and resamples the published DEM onto the crater's display region — which is itself read from the bounding box the Mars Trek imagery publishes, so elevation and imagery cover the same ground — and writes a four-level pyramid from 100 m to 800 m with its provenance, resampling method, valid-data fraction and a datum check against the landing site. Imagery and mission data are fetched live through the app's own server routes, so no credential or third-party origin reaches the browser, and the tile proxy's allow-list is built from the layers registered craters declare rather than hand-written.

Datasets

  • 30 m HRSC DTM Mosaic of Gale
    • Source: ESA Mars Express, Persaud et al. 2021
    • Resolution: 30 m
    • Used for: Gale elevation
    • Source: USGS Astrogeology
    • Resolution: 20 m
    • Used for: Jezero elevation
    • Source: NASA MGS / ESA Mars Express
    • Resolution: 200 m
    • Used for: Regional elevation, datum reference
    • Source: NASA MRO, via Mars Trek
    • Resolution: About 5–6 m/px
    • Used for: Base surface imagery
    • Source: NASA MRO / University of Arizona
    • Resolution: 0.25–0.30 m/px
    • Used for: Close-range detail imagery
    • Source: NASA/JPL public location layers
    • Resolution: One record per drive end
    • Used for: Rover position by sol, landmarks, drive pace
    • Source: NASA/JPL-Caltech, CAB (CSIC-INTA)
    • Resolution: One record per sol
    • Used for: Observed weather at the rover
    • Source: IAU WGPSN / USGS
    • Resolution: Centres to about 600 m
    • Used for: Official feature names and positions

4. Limitations

  • Not mission software, and not validated for operations of any kind.
  • A route is only as good as one 100 m DEM cell: rocks, sand and scarps are invisible to it, and travel time is an estimate at a stated pace, not a prediction.
  • Slope limits and the slope-speed curve are modelling choices the user can change, not published rover specifications.
  • Imagery is greyscale because no verified crater-wide colour dataset exists; nothing is tinted to resemble a photograph, and PLAY's surface image is a rendering of the elevation model, not imagery of Mars.
  • Weather is one moving station, for the sols the public feed carries.
  • No traverse path is drawn for Perseverance and no geologic units for Jezero, because neither has been verified into the app.
  • Vertical datums between tiers are not reconciled; the difference is measured and recorded rather than absorbed.

Credits: NASA/JPL-Caltech · NASA/JPL-Caltech/MSSS · NASA/JPL-Caltech/University of Arizona · NASA/JPL-Caltech/CAB (CSIC-INTA) · ESA/DLR/FU Berlin · USGS Astrogeology Science Center · IAU WGPSN. Imagery served by NASA Solar System Treks. Route planning after Hart, Nilsson and Raphael (1968).
